utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. I hope the technical problems are resolved and we will not be -- we don't have to face any additional problem today. At the outset of our today's hearing, I would like to issue an oral decision. The Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's motion for leave to file an amended Rule 65 ter summary for witness Dusan Janc and confidential Appendix A filed on 9th of March, 2011. In this motion, the Prosecution requests leave to amend its 65 ter witness summary for its witness Dusan Janc. It argues that Witness Janc's proposed additional testimony concerns the provenance and authenticity -- sorry, I -- I will slow down a bit -- of video footage relating to this case which depicts the accused and other alleged JCE members, as well as the reliability of the Croatian intercept material. The Chamber heard the position of the accused last Wednesday. Mr. Gajic, on behalf of Mr. Tolimir, submits that the motion should be denied in relation to the proposed testimony concerning the Croatian intercepts. He argues that the material should instead be tendered through a bar table motion. He also argues that it is inappropriate for an OTP investigator to address the reliability of these documents and such materials should not be introduced through them. With regard to the proposed testimony concerning the video footage, Mr. Gajic suggests that the material be submitted through other witnesses who have direct knowledge of these events. The Chamber understands he does not take a definite position in this respect. Following Mr. Gajic's oral response, the Chamber heard the Prosecution's reply. Mr. McCloskey submits that the proposed testimony is important for establishing the authenticity of these materials with Witness Janc and that the same examination has been done with this witness and other Prosecution investigators such as Witness Frease. Mr. McCloskey argues that the proposed testimony is not prejudicial or untimely. In responding to the Prosecution's reply, Mr. Gajic made further submissions basically reiterating his arguments. In the Chamber's view it is entirely appropriate for Witness Janc to address the issue of reliability of the Croatian intercepts at this stage. The witness's proposed testimony is, prima facie, relevant to and probative of material issues in the case. It will also potentially assist the Chamber since the witness has been involved in the Srebrenica and Zepa investigations. In addition, it is in the interests of the accused that the proposed evidence be presented in this way so as to afford him to cross-examine the witness and the Chamber to ask any additional questions. Lastly, as has been repeated in its written or oral decisions, the Chamber emphasises that it will later accord these materials due weight in terms of its ultimate reliability and probative value, together with all the evidence. For these reasons, the Chamber finds that it is in the interests of justice to allow the amendment of Witness Janc's 65 ter summary. The motion is hereby granted. utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You put your finger on it, Mr. President, I think it is more than slightly longer than usual. General Smith served in the British army for 40 years and retired in 2002. In late January 1995, he began serving as commander UNPROFOR Bosnia and Herzegovina, based in the Residency in Sarajevo. His mission was to support the delivery of humanitarian aid and to carry out the instructions of the Security Council in relation to the exclusions zones and safe areas and to do this amidst a war. His immediate superior was General Janvier who was based in Zagreb. Also in Zagreb, was Yasushi Akashi, who was UN Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali's Special Representative and Smith's political superior. In his headquarters during the relevant period, Smith had a Chief of Staff, General Nicolai, and a military assistant, Colonel Jim Baxter. In Sarajevo was also located Sector Sarajevo, a subordinate UNPROFOR command based in the PTT building, and commanded by General Gobillard. When he took command in January 1995, a cease-fire between the Bosnian Muslims and Serbs had recently been struck and a Cessation of Hostilities Agreement had been signed. As part of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement agreement, joint commissions were set up, through which the two sides could sort out issues that might occur. Smith's predecessor, General Rose, established Joint Commission Observers, known as JCOs, as part of the observer and control mechanism in connection with Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, particularly in Sarajevo. As the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement broke down, the JCOs became more valuable as a means of communications with the enclaves of Srebrenica and Gorazde as it got harder and harder to communicate with those enclaves, and also as forward air controllers. Smith met with Izetbegovic, Muratovic, Silajdzic and Delic on the Muslim side, and Karadzic, Koljevic, Krajisnik and Mladic on the Serb side. Smith would be accompanied by civil affairs officers for these meetings. He also attended meetings with these officials in support of Akashi. Smith's purpose in these meetings was to gain an understanding of their position and intentions and to support Akashi in furthering the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. During these early weeks, Smith developed a thesis to help explain the situation he was seeing and collected information from these meetings and daily reporting from his own officers and the civil side of the UN to prove the hypothesis right or wrong. It was very important for him to have an understanding of the political context, because the position he was in was on the interface between politics and the military. It started to become clear to him that no side to the conflict wanted to make peace at that stage and that the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement would break down. The Muslim side was beginning to gain strength, and their numerical superiority and the arms they were now getting were going to give them an advantage if they started to fight again. On the Serb side, they had gotten so much territory and had so few people that they were overextended, and the only way they could hold the territory was by producing more soldiers. The enclaves, specifically the eastern enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, lay in their rear and required a large number of forces and resources to guard. Smith concluded that not only would the cease-fire break down, but in order to hold the territory they had gained, the Serbs would squeeze the eastern enclaves in order to reduce their significance and free up forces. Smith discussed a number of meetings he had with military and civilian leaders of both sides, from March through September 1995. A record of the meetings was kept by Baxter, and Mladic was always accompanied by another senior VRS officer, frequently the accused. UNPROFOR resupply and humanitarian aid convoys were centrally controlled and restricted by Mladic and his headquarters and were being denied. And among the topics raised by Smith in March and April 1995 were the increasing number of VRS attacks on the safe areas, direct targeting of UNPROFOR personnel, and the disruption of aid convoys. Throughout these meetings, the Bosnian Serb military and political leadership accused UNPROFOR of supplying the defenders in the enclave, especially with fuel. Each of the parties would seek to use the UN and the UN forces to their advantage, which Smith called the hostage and shield situation. The Bosnian Serbs saw the UN as a hostage through which they could control and influence the international community. On the other hand, the Bosnian Muslim side urged a more robust interpretation of the UNPROFOR mandate and the use of NATO to support them as a shield. When the VRS attack on Srebrenica began, Smith was on a two-week leave, but was in daily radio contact with Baxter. Gobillard had assumed command in Smith's absence. Smith was recalled from leave to attend a meeting in Geneva to discuss a report to the Security Council about UNPROFOR. At the meeting, it was reported that a Dutch soldier had been killed and another OP lost. It was the general understanding at that time that what was happening in Srebrenica was further squeezing of the enclave, and a fight over an east/west road to the south of the enclave where the VRS had attacked a DutchBat OP in June with a tank. The consequence of the VRS denials to UNPROFOR during the attack, that the VRS was attacking UNPROFOR or the civilian population, was that it introduced delay into the UN and into the decision making process regarding the use of air power, since both parties were in the habit of blaming the other for various actions and the UN had to verify the information. Smith resumed his leave, but a day later was recalled to Sarajevo because the attack had developed much more strongly. The defence had collapsed and the enclave fell. He arrived in Sarajevo on 13 July. Upon return to Sarajevo, his priorities were the very nearly overwhelming refugee problem at the Tuzla airport and the Dutch hostages and battalion still in Srebrenica. The DutchBat commander was in no way in control of his own circumstances anymore and was "talking from the jail." So he needed to be supported at a level higher than Smith, who was as much in the jail as the DutchBat commander was. Accordingly, Smith attended a meeting in Belgrade on the 15th of July. During that meeting a follow-up meeting was scheduled for 19 July in order to confirm the agreement which was framed in Belgrade and that meeting on the 19th was held at the Jela restaurant and attended by Mladic, the accused, and Indjic. Mladic told Smith that he was meeting in Zepa later that day and sent Smith a letter that night claiming that Zepa had fallen and a surrender arranged. However, Smith treated this claim with considerable suspicion because the actual people doing the fighting were not present at the meeting, and it struck him that the VRS had got the civilians to start to negotiate before they had dealt with the military. Smith attended the London Conference from 20 to 23 July and met with Muratovic in the evening of 23 July. Muratovic was concerned that the Serbs should not have any access to the Muslims from Zepa and with respect to the military-aged men, Smith understood that it was always going to be a problem differentiating between fighters, who are more or less armed, from men of military age who may or may not be fighters, since not all men of military age were members of the armed forces or had the capacity to be a soldier. On 25 July, Smith met Mladic and Gvero again at the Jela restaurant to discuss the outcome of the London Conference, to again press ICRC access to the Srebrenica prisoners, which had not happened, and to discuss Zepa. After the meeting, Smith and Mladic arrived to Zepa separately. Smith met Mr. Torlak, who was a clearly worried man in shirtsleeves, as well as a doctor. The impression the witness had of Torlak was that he had found himself between a rock and a hard place and that the solution was to sign the agreement on 24 July which was put in front of him. Smith returned to Sarajevo late in the evening of the 25th of July and met with Izetbegovic, Muratovic, Masovic, and Dr. Kulovac from Zepa. Smith's priorities were to get UN agencies and personnel on the ground to monitor the situation and to establish what agreement could be reached concerning the POW exchange. Smith also convinced Mladic to permit a CNN team in as a way of avoiding potential excesses. Smith met Mladic again on 26 July at the top of a hill at a Ukrainian check-point. During this time, the VRS officer who was most involved in the operation to remove the civilian population was the accused, who was present on the ground, as well as Mladic. On 27 July, Smith met again with Torlak, Mr. Hajric and Mr. Imamovic, who were considering signing another surrender agreement with Mladic. On the way out of Zepa that last day, he encountered Gvero at a check-point as Gvero was headed into the enclave. Smith next met Mladic in Mrkonjic Grad on the 31st, during a Croatian offensive in the west, which resulted in the ethnic cleansing of Croatian Serbs. By this time, Mladic and his entire high command had moved to the west. On 22 August, Smith met Mladic at Borike near Zepa. And I'll ask General Smith some about that meeting, so I'll just skip part of the summary. And, finally, Smith testified about the role and function of the Main Staff. And he described the structure and functions of the various branchs and other elements of the Main Staff as it acts on the interface between the political elements of a state and the purely military -- to translate the political intentions and desires into military acts. And he further testified, based on his personal observation of the VRS Main Staff, what he observed concerning the command-and-control system that he saw centralised and embodied in the VRS Main Staff. In particular, what he saw in the VRS Main Staff was a relatively small group of people making the decisions at the centre, and there was a capacity to retain this centralised control by splitting off from the main headquarters to put forward elements of the main headquarters alongside the subordinate headquarters in whose area the event in question was taking place and therefore retain that close central control over events. An example of this was in Zepa. By placing his assistant commanders in these forward headquarters, which had the necessary communications links, Mladic was able to have his assistant commanders command in his name across a whole range of responsibilities for the matter for which he was put forth to handle. While Mladic's assistant commanders had specific staff functions, when Smith dealt with the accused or Gvero, he understood each to be a commander, albeit an assistant one, dealing with the matter in hand in the round, and that is how he dealt with them. That concludes my summary, Mr. President. I do have some additional questions for General Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, you discussed your thesis, we just heard a little bit about it in the summary, and part of your thesis was you judged that both sides were prepared to go back to war, active combat. Was there a time-frame during which you judged that the sides wanted the war to be over or by which it needed for their purposes to be over?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I thought that they -- both, for their separate reasons, wanted to see the matter concluding, of course, to their advantage, by the end of that year, 1995. The -- this was for reasons of the availability of resource, as much as anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber has heard, on a couple of occasions, reference to the Carter agreement. Can you tell the Trial Chamber just what the Carter agreement was.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: This was a shorthand for the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. The final stages of reaching that agreement had been chaired and facilitated by President Carter who had flown in right at the -- at that last stage of that process. I can't remember the precise date, but I think it was between Christmas and New Year of 1994, when he was there, and this agreement was finalized and came into -- into being.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as part of your thesis, you testified in Popovic that you had put yourself in Mladic's shoes and anticipated that he would, to use your term, "squeeze the enclaves." And you further testified that, with respect to the VRS restrictions on UNPROFOR resupply and humanitarian aid convoys, that Mladic was very much in charge and that the restrictions and the orders were centrally controlled by him and his headquarters. Do you recall giving that testimony in Popovic, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether these convoy restrictions fit into your thesis.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The -- it's a long time ago since I first started to use this word "squeeze," and -- but it was my word as much to myself as anything else, to describe a process, so that you set out to render this -- this enclave as neutralized as you could, so that it required the very minimum number of your own people on its outside to guard yourself against it, and you could free up the maximum number of forces for deployment elsewhere in your -- in your war. And that -- so controlling the flow of resource into that enclave would achieve that purpose. You would also achieve the purpose of, more specifically, of denying popular support to any military activity that conducted out of that. By -- by pressurising the civil population they, in turn, would pressurise the military, the Bosnian military within that enclave, and secondly, you could use it to squeeze and control the United Nations in this relationship that I called the hostage and shield relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to discuss for a little while the use of air power during your time as commander UNPROFOR, Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I want to just direct your attention to your Popovic testimony. This is transcript page 17601. And just to encapsulate a little bit, and then I will ask you to amplify, you identified three areas of potential use of air power by UNPROFOR through NATO. The first was with respect to the no-fly zones; the second one was close air support in self-defence; and the third was to neutralize the use of, for example, VRS artillery and heavy weapons that were targeting the civilian population or which were violating one of your mandates, the exclusion zones or safe area mandates. Can you explain a little bit more for the Trial Chamber what those three categories really mean. That's a kind of bare bones summary. But if could you expand just a little bit about the differences among those, for example, three uses and perhaps we could talk about a couple of examples that actually happened in -- in May and then obviously in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, there were those three categories. The -- chronologically, they came into force with the no-fly zone category coming in first. This was largely -- which -- it was wholly a NATO responsibility to conduct and -- and was operated from the NATO headquarters in Italy. The -- when that agreement was made and you had forces from one organisation, NATO, operating superimposed over the forces of another organisation, the United Nations, there was clearly the beginnings of a command-and-control problem. And there was also the need to provide added capacity for self-defence to the United Nations forces in case a -- the actions of NATO created a -- a situation in which a UN element on the ground was then threatened. And from that, flowed the need for -- for both those two reasons. There flowed the need for something that came to be called the dual key approach to the handling of air power. This was written down in a NATO document when the safe area and exclusion zones were worked through, and became -- worked through in NATO and the UN, and because now you had to have a capacity for both the commanders to agree that if you were going to fly air attacks to enforce -- air attacks by NATO to enforce the safe area and exclusion zone regime, then both commanders had to initiate this attack by turning their keys. The -- a violation of the no-fly zone was dealt with by NATO in the chain of command and when that was -- circumstances occurred when that -- those air attacks took place, the UN were not part of the chain of command. When a close air support mission, and here I would just draw a distinction, it isn't precise in that it sometimes doesn't quite work like this, but as a general rule, a close air support mission is flown at the request of the people on the ground, and there is an -- a -- a party, usually referred to as a forward air controller, on the ground controlling the attack, and the reason for that is the close proximity of your own forces, and that the situation is directly involving your own forces on the ground. If you are carrying out an air attack, for example, in support of the no -- of the exclusion zone and you wish to attack a specific target, let us say an artillery position, then you may still want to have a forward air controller, but here he is now acting more to indicate the target which might be difficult to see from the ground -- I beg your pardon, difficult to see from the air, than to act as a -- and control the attack in order to ensure the safety of your own forces. If the targets are further away from your own forces, or are easy enough to identify by -- from the air, then the probability is you do not involve a forward air controller at all, and it is conducted by the air force, or air forces, using their own capabilities. I think that's a sort of a -- short guide to those three uses of air power, and in particular in the command-and-control arrangements of it this particular year.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me follow up, General, with a couple of definitional questions and maybe we can look at those examples as they actually took place on the ground in 1995. You've used two terms, "no-fly zone," and I think in the context of what is happening in the Middle East right now, it's certainly a term we're hearing a lot of right now, and you've also used the term "exclusion zone." We have all heard about the safe areas and how the safe areas were constituted, but can you tell the Trial Chamber what do you mean when you are talking with about a no-fly zone, and what do you mean when you are referring to an exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The no-fly zone over Bosnia-Herzegovina was established fairly early on in the -- in the story of this war. My memory is in 1993, but I couldn't be sure of the exact month in that year. But I'm sure we can find it in the record. This was an intervention by the Security Council members of the United Nations who wanted to see the -- a cessation of the use of Bosnian Serb air power on -- specifically on to civilian targets and -- and refugee columns in -- that were coming out of various towns in Bosnia at the time. NATO, as an organisation, whether they were asked or volunteered, I don't recall, but became the body that took on this particular task and, as I've said, it was conducted out -- by the NATO headquarters in -- specific command headquarters was the NATO headquarters in Vicenza in northern Italy. The safe areas were established, but the civil population inside them remained under shell fire on a number of occasions, and the exclusion zone was a further effort by the Security Council and the United Nations to relieve the -- the pressure and stop the direct attacks upon the civil population inside the safe areas. And to do this, a zone, and again my memory may be wrong by a kilometre or two, but I seem to remember it was a 20-kilometre radius, around each of the safe areas was designated. The safe areas were the three eastern enclaves, Sarajevo, Tuzla, and, if I recall, Bihac. But I -- I'm not sure it was the whole of that particular part of the -- of that territory. The safe areas, the exclusion zone, I beg your pardon, were to be free of all heavy weapons which was -- I would -- they were specifically defined, but loosely, anything bigger than an 82-millimetre mortar was considered to be a heavy weapon. These weapons were to be grouped in weapon collection points, and the reason for this was that the United Nations did not want to become partial in this particular war, and that it was agreed that each party should have a capacity to defend itself and the weapons, therefore, would be collected in weapon collections points. For those on the inside of the safe area couldn't take their weapons for 20 kilometres out of it and then have them available for self-defence. So they were grouped inside the safe area in a weapons collection point, and this applied to those on the outside the safe area: In this case, the Bosnian Serbs as well. The weapons were supposed to be, and were until the end of May 1995, under UN supervision within those collection points. The -- and the UN had to agree to them being released, that a case existed for you to have your weapons back for self-defence. And that was, as I recall it, the exclusion zone regime that was extant in the beginning of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn to two uses of NATO air power during your time. The first in May of 1995, and the Trial Chamber has heard a fair amount of testimony about the air-strikes of the 25th of May and 26th of May, 1995, that NATO conducted, targeting, on the 25th, the ammo dump at Pale. The Trial Chamber has obviously heard a lot of testimony about the employment of close air support on 11 July in Srebrenica as well. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber which of the three categories you've just been discussing, each of these events fell into?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The one I know best is the one in May. As you've heard, in July, I'm on leave at that -- or coming back from leave at that particular -- for that particular attack. In May, the situation had been steadily deteriorating during April and May, and we'd reached a stage in -- early in May when I had already requested the use of air power and had it denied in the -- by my superiors in Zagreb. About ten days later, the situation has reached a point where we've had a number of weapons removed from weapon collection points, that is to say, Bosnian Serb army weapons removed by the Bosnian Serbs from weapon collection points under -- in -- in the -- in -- outside of Sarajevo, and there was considerable shelling of the civil areas of Sarajevo. I gained the agreement of my superiors and warned directly, by letter and by broadcast, that if these weapons were not back, put back into the weapons collection point, and the attacks on the civil population didn't stop, then targets would be bombed until these weapons were returned. In consultation with NATO, who had the business of actually carrying out this request, and -- we chose the target, an ammunition depot near Pale. The reason for the choice of this target was that it was far enough away from any civil population so there was a very small probability of any damage to civilians. It was close to the headquarters and capital of the Bosnian Serbs. The evidence of this attack would be impressed upon them. There were a number of ammunition bunkers and by -- it allowed me to escalate into a second attack, since we could start and, in fact, bombed two bunkers and then, if that didn't work, I could move on and bomb more, et cetera. So that was a simple explanation of the rationale of that particular target. And, finally, and not least because of my thesis, I thought that the Bosnian Serbs would be worried about the availability of ammunition, and losing ammunition would be a direct threat to their capacity to conduct their war and achieve their military objectives. And in the light of those, the attacks were initiated. They had no effect, in terms of returning the weapons, and that night all the safe areas, from my memory, were shelled again, all within about an hour of each other, and one of the attacks was particularly lethal, killing some 70 people in Tuzla. And, still, the weapons had not been returned, and so we attacked again, at which -- I can't remember, I think we took out two bunkers on the first attack and four on the next one and this had the immediate reaction of hostage taking, threats of UN personnel having their throats slit, men being chained to the outside of anticipated targets and so forth. The number of hostages was slowly increased over the next 12 hours. I think I've used the word wrong to say slowly, steadily increased to I think some 350 people were hostage within the next 24 hours or so. At which point the resolve of the troop-contributing nations was so weakened that all -- I was told to stop any further attacks. The authority to initiate attacks, excepting close air support for self-defence, was removed from the military commanders and, indeed, from Mr. Akashi, and the -- from the UN side, the authority now rested, after this event, with the Secretary-General himself and nobody else. It -- after this event, we then enter a period of some two weeks, or maybe a little longer, during which negotiations take place to recover the hostages from the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, we started much later than usual, but we -- we must have a break, and I -- I suppose we take our first break now but a shorter break than usual. We will resume at half past at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, General. We left off discussing the air-strikes of the 25th and 26th of May, 1995. Just to literally put them in the -- in the box, was the rationale behind those air-strikes enforcing the exclusion zone, the safe area mandate, self-defence? What was the simple rationale from your perspective for requesting that air power?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The rationale was to enforce the exclusion zones and the safety of the civil population in the safe area regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now you referred in your answer to earlier in May, also requesting air power, but that that was denied. Can you just briefly tell the Trial Chamber what the circumstances were of that earlier request by you for air power.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I'm -- I can't be sure of the dates but it's in the first half of May. There was a tunnel that had been dug by the defenders of Sarajevo under the airport that you may have heard about. And it came out at Butmir on the -- as it were, on the side of the airport away from Sarajevo on the side nearest Mount Igman. On this particular day, at or around midday, the mouth of this tunnel or the buildings in the vicinity of the mouth of this tunnel, was very effectively shelled by the Bosnian Serbs and it killed a number of people. I never got to the bottom, entirely at the bottom, of who were amongst these people who were killed on this particular occasion, but it was -- some were certainly in uniform, and it was -- it clearly a -- a well-targeted attack because it caused an immediate reaction amongst the Bosnians defenders who were demanding air-strikes and that the UN should do something about this, et cetera. I refused to follow this -- these urgings of the Bosnian government on the grounds that were people there in uniform. This particular vicinity was on, or very close to, the front line, and I considered it to be part of, if you like, a military engagement. There was considerable political pressure being put on me, not only by the Bosnian government directly, but from external sources that I should do something about this. I refused to do so for the reasons I've given. However, during the evening, the civil areas of Sarajevo began to be shelled and shelled heavily, to the point that I requested an air attack on the grounds that this was now a -- a denial of the safe area and the exclusion zone regimes. However, having refused to do it on one grounds earlier in the day and now demanding it on another set of grounds was rather too much for the system above me to cope with, and I was -- this particular request was denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General. Let's turn to the 11th of July and understand your caveat that you were probably just about to return from your leave during this period of time.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: You mean the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, I heard you as June.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The use of air support on this occasion fell into which of these categories we've been talking? From your understanding.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The self-defence of NATO, enforcement of the exclusion zone regime, enforcement of the safe area regime, one or more, or none?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: My memory of this event and the reporting of it was that this was a request under the close air support for self-defence of a UN personnel detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in the Popovic trial, you spoke a little bit about distinguishing the concepts of impartiality and neutrality and this is at transcript 17503. If you would, please explain to the Trial Chamber, if you would, how those two concepts are different and how that difference played out, in your experience, for example, during the employment of this air power that we've been talking about? If you wanted to use any of those examples, or another example, if you've got a better one.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: These two words, it had been my experience that these two words tend to be used in the same breath and almost as synonyms, and I didn't -- and I don't think that that is the case, and I -- and particularly, in the circumstances I found myself as a commander, I thought it was very important to make sure that I, at least, understood what I -- what was meant by those words, and so that in some of these rather difficult situations where you're standing in the middle of someone else's fight, you can work out just what to do and achieve the object that you've been set. My -- my way of understanding it is by referring myself, if you like, to this following example. If I was a medical officer in the British Army in a war, I would clearly not be neutral. I would be in the British Army, I would be wearing a British Army uniform, and I would be marching under the flag, under the Union Jack. But my duty as a doctor was to carry out my profession impartially, and thus if a casualty was brought in, an enemy that was one of my enemies, I -- my duty was to treat him impartially according to his wounds, and if his wounds were greater and of greater urgency than those of a soldier of my own army, I would -- I would be correct, and it would be my duty as a doctor, to treat the enemy soldier first, because his need was greater than that of my own soldier. So holding that example in mind, I approached the situation where we were to be neutral, but the situation would create the situation where one's actions, if you like, had to be considered within that impartial definition as opposed to one's position of neutrality. And so if a situation occurred where one saw, for example, great need of a population for supply of -- of humanitarian goods, then your business was to supply to those people who needed it, regardless of which side they were on. Equally, if something, some sanction such as the no-fly zone was breached, then that situation had created the situation where you had to -- I, as the commander, had to exercise my understanding of my impartiality in this case, in which case my duty lay with re-imposing the exclusion zone, or whatever it was that had been breached.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has heard a lot of testimony about the use of NATO air power. Again, in May; in July; and then, ultimately, in September of 1995. The targets of that air power in each of those cases were Bosnian Serb targets. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber why, during the same period of time, let's say from the beginning of 1995 through September of 1995 when there were Muslim offences from outside of Sarajevo, threats from Muslim officers in the case of Zepa to -- to kill Ukrainian peace keepers, why NATO air power wasn't employed against the Muslim army or forces.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: In the first instance, the use of air power was not to be understood as the immediate response to every particular situation. It was a -- it was something that one used or was expected to be used sparingly, if at all. So it isn't a solution to everything. Nor is it a solution to everything in that it has its own characteristics and it has to be applied within its, as it were, capabilities. In particular, the interpretations of what it meant in using air power in the case of self-defence or in -- close air support in self-defence -- is there is a time matter that has to be understood and considered. The first is these aircraft were not held in a sort of permanent orbit over the UN. They had to be requested and it takes time for them to fly out there and be there. Secondly, as I have explained there has to be a forward air controller to actually conduct the attack and if you haven't got the planes and/or you haven't got the forward air controller there, then you can't apply this weapon in those circumstances. And, finally, the understanding of what self-defence meant was taken broadly from the -- if you like, understanding in civil law that if you're not actually being attacked at the time, then you're no longer able to say that you need close air support for self-defence. So if the attack had occurred, you couldn't apply this particular capability in -- for that reason. If the man you were trying to defend was no longer being shot at or whatever, he was no longer requiring civil defence and you couldn't uses it punitively after the event. So those limited -- the use of air power in a number of cases where, on the face of it, an incident was occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. General, I want to turn your attention to Zepa for a little while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wonder if you could clarify for me at page 32, in line 15 to the end, Mr. Thayer has asked you to explain: "Can you explain to the Trial Chamber why during this same period of time, let's say from the beginning of 1995 through September 1995, when there were Muslim offences from outside of Sarajevo, threats from Muslim forces ... why NATO air power wasn't employed against the Muslim army or forces?" You have explained quite clearly and eloquently what needs to be in place for the air power to be called. But I think I have missed your answer as to exactly why, in the particular instance that Mr. Thayer has explained, why air power was not used or if it was used at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't used at all, and I'd have to have a specific -- I have used examples there as some of the reasons why it might not have been used. But without a specific case, I find it difficult to -- he did mention one specific case, didn't he, in Zepa? There, the -- if -- the case I can recall, either I or General Gobillard, I think it was General Gobillard, got hold of the then-prime minister Sacirbey and invited him to get a control of his people in Zepa and that took -- that dealt with that problem that way rather than calling in air power. I also think it was happening at night which is a further complication in these matters. But I can't remember the timing very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In -- in Popovic, General, you described how Colonel Karremans, the DutchBat commander on the ground there, by the -- by the 11th of July was, in your words, "talking from the jail" and in the summary I read out, I repeated your words that you were in the jail, just as much as he was. And I think we all understand what you're talking about there. My question to you is: In Zepa, when you go down there on the 25th, were you in the jail, as you were in -- or as you and Colonel Karremans were back in Srebrenica on the 11th of July and afterwards? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The short answer is, no, we were nothing like as much. In the Zepa case, we were nothing like as much in the jail as I thought Karremans and, to that extent, me, were in -- in the Srebrenica case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why not, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Although we'd been presented with the fait accompli of the Bosnian Serb attack, the presence of Bosnian Serbs in the enclave and so forth, we were present and had a great deal more freedom of action and movement than in the Srebrenica case. Secondly, we had the media there. There was, as it were, a witness of other agencies, which included the ICRC. We had the -- the male population had, in the main, taken to the hills and were not in the same circumstances as those that I understood at the time in Srebrenica, all having been taken prisoner. I just couldn't gain access to them. So the -- the context was -- was different to that of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you in a position to, as it were, reclaim the enclave or kick Mladic out?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: No. I was in no position to do that. To that extent, I had been presented with this fait accompli.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, how about the Ukrainian company commander on the ground in Zepa? The Trial Chamber has heard about Colonel Dudnik. Was he talking from the jail?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. He and his men had been -- were, to a large extent, in the Karremans' position, first with the -- with the defenders and then with the attackers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now you just referred to the male population from Srebrenica and not gaining access to those people. And in your testimony, you referred on a couple of occasions to 2.000 Muslim men who you are repeatedly asking General Mladic to give ICRC and UNHCR access to but who remain unaccounted for. And that's, for example, at transcript page 17536. Do you recall referring on a number of occasions to these 2.000 men that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at the time, what was your understanding of where these men had been seized and where they were being held during this period of time in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: My understanding is that they had been taken at Srebrenica after the pocket had collapsed, that they had been separated out from the women and children, and that they -- they were being held in Bratunac. And my memory is that we thought they were being held in a football stadium there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, ultimately, when ICRC was granted access, do you recall what the ICRC representatives were shown?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I -- I seem to remember being told that they were finally granted access sometime in early August, but that might have been when I was told as opposed to when they got access. And they were shown some empty -- what one might call detention facilities but they weren't convinced that anyone had necessarily been there. And they certainly didn't have any of those 2.000 men there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you also testified about your knowledge that, contemporaneous with your involvement down in Zepa, there were ongoing discussions, meetings at the Sarajevo airport about a potential prisoner exchange. Do you recall that testimony, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember how, or if at all, the whereabouts of, for example, these 2.000 men who you were trying to get access to figured into these meetings and discussions, trying to effect an all-for-all exchange?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I have a vague -- a not very comprehensive memory of this -- these negotiations. They were -- the idea of a prisoner exchange started fairly early in the Zepa incident. There was a procedure of -- that was conducted between the parties at the airport for dealing with prisoner exchanges and the political affairs element of the UN headquarters, in my headquarters, was responsible for facilitating these talks between the parties on prisoner exchanges at the airport. And my memory of this negotiation was that it kept stalling on what did "all" mean? And the Bosnian Serbs essentially didn't think that Srebrenica's prisoners were part of the exchange, part of "all," and the Bosnian government considered that they most definitely did. And the debate kept stalling over that issue. But I -- beyond knowing that it was going on all the time and reached no result, I don't recall much more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. We already talked a little bit, if you will, about this Dr. Kulovac, who you met in Zepa. Do you remember meeting him at some point in Sarajevo during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I met him late one night, or very early one morning, after he'd come out with a busload of wounded and the very sick, of people from Zepa. And I think I met him in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall, General, whether Mr. Kulovac, after reaching Sarajevo, stayed in Sarajevo, or did he get back on one of the buses and return to Zepa during this time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think he returned, but I couldn't be absolutely sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at video-clip, if we could, please, this is from P594. It's just going to be a couple of seconds of footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I, at this point put a question to the witness. You just mentioned the Presidency. You said, "I think I met him in the Presidency."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This was a large building in which Izetbegovic had his -- his offices and so forth known as the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Sarajevo itself, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. And the place you resided in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Residency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Residency. And what kind of building was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's -- was a substantial house in its own grounds in the centre of Sarajevo. It, I understood, dates or dated, the name at least, from about a century before when people moved about the Austro-Hungarian empire, there was places called the Residency in most large provincial capitals in which visiting officials and so forth would stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to play some video and again this is at -- this is P594. We're going to start at approximately 46 minutes into the video. About 20 seconds of video and then I want to go back to a little clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We've paused at 46 minutes, 15.9 seconds. Can you identify anybody in this still that we have here on the screen, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: My military assistant, the then-Colonel Baxter, is in -- is the balding head in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Holding a notebook or a pad in his hand, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Holding the notebook in his hand and with his right hand in the air and slightly out of focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue rolling this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have paused at 46 minutes, 25.9 seconds. Can you identify anybody in this still.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I have Mr. Mladic, or General Mladic, is the man with his arm and watch across the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recognise anybody else?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I think that's Mr. -- that's Indjic back right behind the -- Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With the moustache?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could start the clip again, please, and just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're at 46 minutes, 7.0 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've stopped at 46 minutes, 9.8 seconds. There's an individual in the immediate foreground with a beard and a blue shirt. Do you know who that is? Can you recognise that man?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: From memory, that's the doctor that we've talked about just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We're done with this exhibit. With respect to Zepa, the last thing I'd like to take you through, General, is a packet of reports from David Harland, and there's going to be a collective groan from some people in the courtroom; we've worked with this exhibit before. It's a collection of 18 reports that we've looked at with other witnesses, and I want to show you about five, fairly quickly, if I could, and this is 65 ter 2438. The first report is at page 39 of e-court, which is page 30 in the B/C/S. Great. We can see, for the record, that we're at tab 8 in both versions. If we could just go to the next page in both. That should be page 31 in B/C/S. Can we try 31 in B/C/S if -- we're there? Oh. Okay. I'll just read into the record the portions we're interested in. There's not too much. I thought there was a translation available for this. We can see here, we have a 25 July 1995 report from David Harland to John Ryan and General Gobillard, and the subject is: Zepa negotiations, report number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We see that it refers to an airport meeting between 1.30 and 5.30 this day. There's a reference to the elements of a form agreement being expected. And if we go down to the very bottom, we see that there's a reference to Harland reporting the results of the meeting to, among other people, General Smith's ADC. And who is this referring to, your ADC?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: He is called Captain Lavender. Subordinate to one's military assistant, I had an aide de camp who was this Captain Lavender. And if I was out and about I would be accompanied by my military assistant, and the ADC would act as the long stalk back in the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's a reference above to a tentative agreement being reached at the airport to be signed the next day, the 27th, but at the bottom of this page, it reads: "I learned that General Smith and General Mladic had apparently reached an agreement between themselves, under which ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's a reference in subparagraph 1 to medevacs from Zepa would begin immediately. "2, 60 UNPROFOR troops would proceed to Zepa; and, 3, evacuation of civilians to the area of Kladanj would begin tomorrow." My question, General, is: This agreement that Harland is reporting that he received information from, do you recall on the 25th reaching any such agreement with General Mladic; and if you did, was it verbal, was it written down? What was it, what -- what's this report referring to, if you can remember? And is it accurate, I guess, first of all?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sure it's accurate in the sense that this is what Harland understood was the situation at the time. I've -- my experience of his reporting was that it was -- it was good. What -- the first thing is that the agreements were going to have be made between the Bosnians and the Bosnian Serbs, not between me and -- and anyone else. I was there to see that agreement was reached and that the -- if at all possible, and that the -- the civilian population were looked after and so forth. My second comment is that I -- at this stage, I don't think we had -- I think those would have been, if you like, lines on which people -- we were -- agreement looked as though it might be being formed but I don't think we had reached the point at that stage of actually reducing anything to writing or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, when we had the other witness who was here testifying about this packet of documents, I think we're all agreed the Defence position was they didn't have an objection, under those circumstances, to the then witness testifying and having those reports that he testified about coming into evidence. I'm trying to complete this document so we can tender the whole thing and I would again invite the Trial Chamber to invite the Defence to seek their position on this additional report and the other four that I will be showing General Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sure the Defence will express their objections if there are any. You should continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll just continue then, Mr. President. May we have page 74 in e-court, please. And this is page 51 in the B/C/S. For the record, we're at tab 15 of this packet. If we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see this is another report from David Harland, this time dated 31st of July. And this one is headed: Zepa negotiations, report number 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll need to go to the next page in the -- in both versions. And one more in the B/C/S, please. And again, just one more in the B/C/S after that. And, I'm sorry, one more page in the B/C/S. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can't see the first page in B/C/S. I can't see it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was there for a short moment. Then Mr. Thayer moved to the next and the next and the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm trying to get to the -- to the actual beginning of the report, Mr. President. For some reason, as we saw the translation chopped the B/C/S of the cover page into three separate pages, so the part I want to focus on for General Smith is here on this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And if there's a need at the end of dealing with this document, we can go back to the first page and enable Mr. Tolimir to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very easily. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, we can see here again this is dated the 31st of July. In the second paragraph here, we can see that Harland reports: "In the morning, I spoke with General Smith and gave him my opinion that the present impasse benefits only the Serbs: Zepa is neutralized, and UNPROFOR is sitting on a remote piece of Serb-controlled territory with 150 potential hostages." And then we can all see the rest here. I won't read it into the record. But if you'll take a moment, read to the bottom of the page, and when you need it turned --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: You can turn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I think we can stay in the B/C/S, because this text is captured on the B/C/S page. According to Harland, you've reported to him that you had met with General Mladic near Banja Luka on this day, the 31st of July, and that the entire Serb high command, including Mladic, Gvero, Milovanovic, and Tolimir, appeared to have moved from the Srebrenica-Zepa area to Banja Luka. And we see here, in Roman numerals I through VI, Harland's account of what you are reporting to him, Mladic told you --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- on the 31st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do we need to go to the next page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If General Tolimir has had an opportunity, certainly, we are at the last paragraph of this section.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And my first question is: Does this report accurately reflect your conversations, both with Mr. Harland and I'll just start there, instead of putting two questions to you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: As far as I can remember them, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And secondly, your meeting with General Mladic on the 31st.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- as I recall those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we see here in the seconds-to-the last paragraph, Colonel Coiffet noting that the Sector Sarajevo commander on the ground was unable to render any assistance to the residual Bosnian civilian population in the hills, and favoured withdrawal." Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that's about, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you've -- the -- the male population, certainly those of military age, with the exceptions of one or two had all withdrawn into the hills, whether they were armed or not. And these are mentioned as the Bosnian fighters in the hills by -- in the report of what Mladic told me, and these people were not -- had no intention of surrendering to the Bosnian Serbs, whether they were armed or not. And I was maintaining a presence until I was confident that they -- that -- that the situation had developed to the point that they were either not there or were no longer likely to be rounded up by the Bosnian Serbs. And we're coming to the point when I'm about to withdraw, not least because of circumstances that had started to develop in the west of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we can see here in Roman numeral III that General Mladic is reporting to you - and we need to go back to the previous page in B/C/S to capture Roman numeral III. We can see that General Mladic is reporting to that he has already got information that, in his words, the Bosnian fighters in the hills around Zepa were attempting to break out into three directions: Towards Kladanj, west, and then east, over the river, to Serbia and south towards Gorazde. Did you come into this information independent of Mladic or was he the only source that you had at this time for that information?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: He was my only source of information about the directions, Kladanj and Gorazde. But I was aware -- and I don't think I shared this information with anybody like David Harland, so he wouldn't have known, that there were negotiations going on between Carl Bildt and the Serbians in Belgrade to, as it were, receive these people from Zepa as refugees under the auspices of the ICRC. And part of my reason for continuing to maintain a presence in the pocket was to wait until I'd seen that -- that these negotiations had shown fruit and -- and that people were starting to cross the river, at which point there became less and less reason for me to keep people in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 78 in e-court and page 57 in the B/C/S. And, again, I don't think we've got a translation for the B/C/S, but it's a one-page document. I just want to look at a couple portions of it. We can see, for the record, that we're looking at tab 16, so if we could go to the next page, please. It's a document headed: The situation in Zepa as of 2 August. It states, "Civil affairs, the present situation in Zepa to be as follows ..." And it starts off, we can see, saying: "The village of Zepa is empty expect for a few Serb soldiers." There's a reference to looting. And if we could skip the next paragraph and I want to focus on two other paragraphs. The third paragraph, and I'll just read this into the record for the benefit of the accused. The third paragraph reads: "The upland interior of the Zepa enclave appears not to have been overrun by the Serbs. It is estimated that perhaps 2.000 people remain in this area, most of whom are believed to be men of military age; and some of whom are believed to be civilians." Now the document we just looked at indicated that General Mladic referred to all of the men from Zepa in the hills as fighters and -- and claimed that there were no civilians left in the hills. We have here the civil affairs belief that some of the men in the hills are, indeed, civilians. Do you recall hearing this information that the UN believed there were civilians among these men and where that information came from, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I -- I held a similar view -- I -- it -- that they wouldn't all be fighters, and although I have been talking about the men of military age and this report talks of the military age, I was quite - you know, I wouldn't have been surprised to find women amongst them, particularly younger women. The -- it -- they weren't classified in my mind as only fighters. They were people who didn't want to be in any way -- be moved through Serb hands into -- or run the risk of being moved through Serb hands, the Serb ground, Serb -- Bosnian Serb land into Sarajevo or Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we can scroll down just a little bit. And, sir, why wouldn't you have been surprised, as you said, to have learned that there were particularly young women among these people in the hills?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Because there was talk of and a certain amount of evidence in previous cases of rape, of -- of women being raped.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has heard a lot of testimony about the movement of the civilian population out of Zepa on the 25th, 26th, 27th, and then a little bit on the 28th. Do you recall whether you actually received any reports of any rapes occurring during that transportation?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: No. I had no reports of any rapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the next-to-last paragraph on this page. It's the one right above the paragraph that's a little obscured. It states: "The Serbs have not allowed UNPROFOR into the Bosnian-controlled area of the pocket and have never granted any freedom of movement other than between OP-2 and Zepa village, both at the south-west corner of the enclave." Is this statement correct, General? Is this how you experienced it? Or is it not correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: No, that's how I experienced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let's go to page 81, please, in e-court. And I don't think we have the translation back yet for this one either. For the record, we're at tab 17 in the English version. If we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a couple of quick questions about this document and then the last one in the pact. We can see from the date, it's 2 August 1995. Report from David Harland. The subject is: Zepa negotiations, report number 15. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please. And if we could scroll down just a little bit more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's a reference to a meeting with yourself and General Gobillard about the French forces remaining in the Zepa pocket. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber what is going on, what's being discussed in this report?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Can we go to the next ... next page? Or is it just --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is a next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So if we can go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll see in a moment, General, the letter that is referred to in the previous page that you sent to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah. I can talk to it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't know what this is all about. There is no translation. The question is ambiguous, so I really don't know what to think about all this, what this is all about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Thayer, you should read that part in the record so that Mr. Tolimir receives a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President. The page we have is headed: Assessment. And the assessment reads: "Once the evacuation of civilians from the Serb-controlled part of the Zepa pocket was completed (on 27 July), UNPROFOR was not able to do much for the people who remained. The Serbs did not allow UNPROFOR into the Bosnian-controlled part of the pocket, and there was no evacuation or surrender agreement to implement. Thus, UNPROFOR's people in Zepa were acting only as potential hostages. "It seems that the remaining population of Zepa will have to fend for themselves. Most will presumably try to flee. And most of those are likely to be killed or captured."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what's going on that this report is reporting on?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: There's three things coming to a head here. I am in the knowledge of these negotiations, of which I'm not sharing with my command, and particularly not with my civil affairs officer is making sure I've still got some people in Zepa in case those negotiations fail. From memory, I have evidence that people are now crossing the Drina and going into Serbia at about this time. At the same time, France -- I've got Ukrainian forces in the pocket, I have a few British forces, but the bulk of the force is a French infantry company. And at this point, France is getting concerned about the potential risk that their own forces are under in this pocket as potential hostages to fortune. Since I'm going in and out of the pocket, I am less concerned than France. And the -- and then you have the need to pull everyone out all together and bring them out and cleared through the Bosnian Serb territory to get back to Sarajevo, and that's got to be organised as well. And the reporting by David Harland is privy to the problems of extracting everybody, privy to the concerns of France being rehearsed in New York, but he is not aware that I'm hanging on until I'm confident that people have started to cross the Drina. Somewhere around that day, I'm able to start to withdraw. I think I -- I want to go about 24 hours after the French want everyone to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with respect to this assessment that I just read into the record, in July of 1995, when this is being written, did you share this assessment, or is there anything in this assessment with which you disagree?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I was less worried about everybody -- where does he say: "Most will presumably try to flee. Most of these will likely be killed or captured." I was not sharing that because I understood that the back door was open over the Drina and into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could just go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have here a letter from you personally to General Mladic. It's dated the 2nd of August at 1120 Bravo, 1995. The subject is: Withdrawal from Zepa. You write: "Further to our meeting on the 31st of July 1995, it is clear that people are now breaking out of the enclave of Zepa. It is judged that there is little left for UNPROFOR to do. "As a result, orders have been given to me to withdraw UNPROFOR from Zepa." And then you request convoy clearance. And you end up by saying: "Should any more members of the civilian population appear, I am sure that you will continue to guarantee access to UNHCR, ICRC, and UN civil affairs personnel who we intend to base in Pale." Do you recall sending this letter to --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Last report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 86. And there is a translation, which is at page 61. For the record, we're looking at tab 18. If we could go to the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see this is another report from David Harland. It's dated the 3rd of August. And the subject is: Zepa. And we can see it's report number 16. I note, if we look at the -- it's to John Ryan and General Gobillard. And we see in the information section, it says Antonio Pedauye, chief of mission UNPROFOR, HQ Sarajevo. First of all, trust me, we've got the correct spelling after all that, if we agree, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just briefly, what is the chief of mission, UNPROFOR headquarters? What was that position in?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The civil and military chains of command in the UN at that time, and I don't know whether it's still the case now, were parallel, and each reporting in parallel back to New York, the -- with the military setting up their headquarters and sharing the same headquarters with the civil component. So in Zagreb you have the SRSG, the Special Representative for the Secretary-General, and the Force Commander. In Sarajevo, you have the head of mission and -- or chief of mission and UNPROFOR commander. And now it -- although you share the same headquarters, you're reporting separately. So you can see Harland as the civil affairs chief in Sector Sarajevo with his military commander, commander Sector Sarajevo, Gobillard. He is reporting in parallel to Gobillard. Gobillard is reporting to me and Harland is reporting to Pedauye, and so on up the line to New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now if we go to the next page in the B/C/S but stay where we are in English, please. We can see that it's an update, and Mr. Harland reports: "There are now no international personnel in the Zepa area." And that: "The last 203 UNPROFOR military personnel have withdrawn from the area in three convoys." And he details the movement of those personnel and then states: "No UNHCR, ICRC, NGO, or other international agencies are present." And if we could go to the next page just in the English. He is reporting further that: "With the UNPROFOR withdrawal from Zepa, this office now has no firsthand source of information on the situation in Zepa." Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether this information, as reported by Mr. Harland, is accurate, based on your experience in the ground?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I -- that's -- remind me, it was the 3rd of August again?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, General.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: That's the situation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think, Mr. President, I think I have already exceeded by two-hour estimate. I do have one document that I passed over in our discussion of the use of air power that I'd like to show General Smith and then I do have another topic which will be at least 20 minutes, I think. And I'd ask the Court for this extra time on these topics which I think will be of benefit to the -- to the Trial Chamber. Particularly, I want to discuss with General Smith some of his observations of how the Main Staff operated in his experience, which weren't gone into during his Popovic testimony, and I'd like to take all together, I think about another half-hour to complete that portion of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, firstly we must have our second break now, and I must express my concern. This is really very unsatisfactory. You should be able to estimate your time you need in examination-in-chief and you must be aware that most of the testimony of this witness is already in evidence. We come back to that question. We adjourn and resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, you may continue, but finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will. May we have 65 ter 6039 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the English translation to come up, what we can see on the left and on UNPROFOR stationery but in B/C/S has been translated for our purposes on the other side. So if you would just take a moment and read the English translation of this letter that, on its face, indicates it was sent from you to General Mladic on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And could we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you're done reading the document, General, please just let us know.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What is the purpose of sending this letter to General Mladic on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: It is to remind him and place on record, again, that the -- that this was a safe area, it had UN forces in it, and there were provisions for their self-defence and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you refer to a number of UN Security Council Resolutions in this letter, numbers 836, 856 and 1004. We're not going to conduct a pop quiz here as to what each of these specific resolutions stated. But generally speaking, can you tell the Trial Chamber what these resolutions that you're citing to here provided.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: These, from memory, are those to do with the safe areas' exclusion zones, and the exclusion zones, and they provided for the protection of the civil population within those areas and the exclusion of heavy weapons and so forth from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with respect to the potential or recourse to NATO air power in the events of violations, was that mentioned in any of these three resolutions, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I'd have to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from your recollection was the potential use of NATO air power something that was explicitly addressed by the UN Security Council in some resolution, whatever number it might have been?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 6039, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document shall be assigned exhibit number P2087. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what about the previous package?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think, to be on the safe side, I'd like some time to go through each of those tabs - I've done almost all of them - just to make sure we've got no problems with them and then I can come to you, and I think, save some more time, by doing it later, when we're ready to tender the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn your attention now to some of your observations of not only various Main Staff officers, but how they interacted among themselves and with their lower echelons during your time in Bosnia. You testified to some degree concerning the relationship between the political leadership and the military leadership in Popovic, but I want to spend a little bit more time in an area that we didn't get into in -- in the last case. The first area I want to explore with you is the -- your observations of the individual armies; specifically the VRS and the Armija, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You noted in the Popovic trial that the VRS had more professional and trained officers than the other two armies, and I presume you're referring to the ABiH and the Croatian forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in formulating your thesis and observing the VRS and the Armija, did you come to some assessment of their relative strengths and weaknesses? Again, we've already addressed in the prior trial to some degree their officer corps. But let's focus for a minute, for example, on their weapons, in particular their heavy weapons. If you can provide us with a little bit of your assessment based on your observations and information.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
