utterances.text: The -- it was my observation that the -- that the former Yugoslavian army, when things began to break up and the underpinning situation that led to this war began to develop, the -- when the Yugoslavian army fell apart, the bulk of the professional officers went towards the Bosnian Serb forces. That is to say, those that were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were to be found in the Bosnian Serb army. And with them, went the larger proportion of the weapons, heavy weapons in particular, and the associated ammunition that was available in Bosnia-Herzegovina was in the hands of the Bosnian Serb forces. In addition to the heavy weapons, and not least by virtue of having the -- a higher proportion of the professional officers, they also had the, if you like, an extant staff system - I refer to it, I think, as a nervous system - upon which to build an army. The -- these -- this all, in comparison, to the Bosnians. So the Bosnian army lacked, in comparison, the heavy weapons, the same -- a degree of the cadre of professional officers and this nervous system upon which to build an army. What the Bosnian army had was greater numbers. It -- it was -- it could -- it was numerically stronger and with a smaller area to defend.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, the Trial Chamber has heard a lot of testimony about raids conducted by armed combatants, Muslim combatants from inside the Srebrenica enclave outwards towards targets outside the Srebrenica enclave. And it's, again, uncontested by the Prosecution that that activity occurred and that it occurred in 1995 during the relevant time-period. My -- and it's -- again, further, not a matter of dispute from the Prosecution that there were weapons coming into the enclave by helicopter and other means, to arm the Muslim forces who were in the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. My question to you, General, is: Number one, do you recall receiving reports of some of these activities, these attacks, these raids from inside the enclave outwards?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do recall receiving reports. One, in particular, precedes the attack on Srebrenica in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from your understanding, from the information that you were provided at the time, did you understand -- or can you provide the Trial Chamber with your understanding of the size and nature of these forces or these groups that were conducting these attacks and raids from inside the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: They were -- let me start with, it -- it -- it was clear to me, if only by deduction, that it was the Bosnian army's strategy to keep the enclaves active and a nuisance, at the very least, to the Bosnian Serbs and that they were trying to get weapons and they were succeeding in getting weapons, and so forth, into the enclaves. The -- at enclave level as opposed to Bosnian army level, the object of these attacks was much more to gain food and -- as well as being a nuisance. So you were raiding to get supplies and so forth into the -- as well as being just a nuisance and in the rear areas of the Bosnian Serbs. And the bulk of these raids, I don't think were conducted by bigger groups than plus or minus 50 men on any one occasion was my impression of these attacks when they occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether it was reported to you that the targets of these attacks were military and -- as well as civilian?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I don't recall. All of these reports of Bosnian military raids came to us from the Bosnian Serbs, and they reported them as attacks on -- as both military attacks and civil attacks, in that they stole sheep or something like that. But they were also said to be military attacks on Bosnian Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall it being reported to you that civilians were killed during any of these attacks as well?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I can -- I -- as I recall it, the attack in July that preceded the attack in -- the Bosnian Serb attack on Srebrenica had -- there were civilian casualties in that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You're referring to an attack in July. Was that the attack on a settlement by the name of Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that was its name, yes. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if I told you and I don't think I'm going to get any dispute from the Defence that that attack occurred in late June, does that sound about right, or do you think that was in July --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: No, it could have been late June. I remember it as an event that was the -- if you like, the -- that starts the process that leads to the attack on -- on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Is my memory of the chronology.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to now turn your attention to some of your observations of the actual officers of the VRS. You've testified at great length about your contacts with General Mladic during, in particular, the time of the Zepa operation. Can you describe the level of control that General Mladic appeared to you to have over his army?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: It -- as far as I could see, he had complete control. He, in a -- in -- exercised command directly and firmly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Trial Chamber the levels in the army at which you saw that control exercised that you've described your contacts with members of the high command, as we might refer to it, or the Main Staff. But did you have opportunities to observe his level of control of subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, a particular case comes to mind is when I'm cleared to visit Srebrenica in March of 1995, and we get, as we're driving there, we get lost and we finish up at a Serb check-point and are halted there. And my liaison officer is able to talk quite quickly. We're -- within 20 minutes, half an hour, directly to General Mladic from that check-point and have us cleared away and from the check-point and on to Srebrenica. The -- he -- my observation was that he and the Bosnian -- the Bosnian Serb army he commanded was what I would characterise as a very centralised command system, in which the main headquarters kept their hand very firmly on what was going on around them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, General, were you able to gauge, based on your observations of General Mladic and his senior officers, the degree to which he would tolerate any breakdown in the chain of command within his army?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: My impression was that he wasn't about to tolerate any breakdown. He wanted to be in command and in control. He exercised command through his -- as I observed it, through his immediate subordinate commanders and senior staff officers. And within his command system and the construction of his main headquarters, he had the capacity to split off forward headquarters. I'm not sure what they were called by the Bosnian Serb army, but I -- that was my name for them. And you could put, as it were, a Main Staff headquarters (forward) alongside a subordinate to make sure that things were going exactly as you would wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. For my last series of questions, I want to direct your attention, in particular, to your assessment based on your observations of the accused, General Tolimir, and his role and place in General Mladic's army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 27 -- I beg your pardon. 7247 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We'll be looking at a copy of your 1996 witness statement. I think it's easier just to pop that up and ask you some questions about what is in there. So if we could have 7247 in e-court. Do you recognise your signature on the front page of this witness statement, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 6, please, in both the English and the B/C/S. I'd like to focus on the -- perfect. Thank you. And in the B/C/S, I think we'll have to scroll down a little bit. A little bit more. Okay perfect?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We see the last sentence of the first full paragraph, you state: "I believe in terms of the RS military hierarchy, Gvero was second fiddle Tolimir, who Mladic described as 'my right-hand man.'"

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the occasion when General Mladic told you this or was this something that was reported to you, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I don't remember the occasion. But I doubt I would have said it as a quote if he hadn't said it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we continue into the next paragraph, you describe what you believe or understood was General Tolimir's position as head of security for the Bosnian Serb army. And you note that he played a prominent and open role in the cleansing of the Zepa enclave where he was seen to be in personal charge of the organisation of assembling buses and putting refugees on to them. Do you see that portion, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: From your testimony in the Popovic case, am I correct that you never went down into the village of Zepa when the removal of the population was occurring; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So this information here about General Tolimir being seen to be in personal charge of the organisation of assembling buses and putting refugees onto them, what is the source of your statement in this witness statement [overlapping speakers]?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: It would have been the political affairs officers - Ed Joseph and I can't remember the name of the other one, he was a Ukrainian - who were down there, and a -- and I had a JCO detachment down there as well, and they would have reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The Ukrainian, was that Mr. Bezruchenko, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this JCO detachment, can you provide the names of the detachment of --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: No. I have a memory that it's the commander of my JCOs was there. He was a Major Wood, but he may not have been there all the time, or been a witness to that particular incident, but he might easily have been the person who reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now you go on in the statement, and you report, or you state that Tolimir was a trusted and close confidante of Mladic. What's your basis for saying that in the statement, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, on most -- on many occasions when I had met Mladic, General Tolimir was there as well. You saw there the interplay between them. You witnessed them inter-react. There were one or two occasions when I can remember them having an argument, you know, we were talking across the table, Mladic and I, and then suddenly Tolimir was having an argument with Mladic. That sort of relationship. This was close. And then he was being -- he would be used, that is to say, General Tolimir, you would find that he had been put out to, you know, in one of these forward headquarters that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is it, General, about Generals Mladic and Tolimir arguing in front of you which makes you draw the conclusion that they had a close relationship or helps you draw that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it was the body language and the tone. This was a -- this was, you know, rather closer to being equals and so forth, rather than a direct subordinate. They were -- they were -- they -- you could see that this was an a pair operating together, if you will, rather than a -- a straightforward hierarchical structure with one doing what he was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The last sentence of this paragraph, you state: "I would expect to find that Tolimir had a significant role in all BSA actions including Srebrenica, and in rallying the situation when the BSA Defence collapsed in western Bosnia." Again, can you explain to the Trial Chamber what your basis for making this statement in your witness statement is?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, what he was in charge of, of security and by inference, intelligence and so forth, was -- is central to the command process on -- of an army, particularly in circumstances such as the Bosnian Serbs were in. So what he was doing was -- was an essential function within the command process in the first place. Secondly, I'd seen him, as it were, at Zepa, and I didn't know he'd been at Srebrenica at the time, but the same structures and organisation would have, I suppose, have applied in Srebrenica as it did a few weeks later, a few days later, in fact, at Zepa. And then, as it -- the business of the west -- what went on in western Bosnia, to some extent, that was formed from a conversation with General Tolimir that he and I had had in - it's either the one in October that's mentioned there in that paragraph, or subsequently - where we discussed that particular time and how he'd been very nearly captured while trying to organise the defences on the western side of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, is the problem solved?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would kindly ask General Smith and the Prosecutor to slow down. It's impossible to follow their words in two languages if they continue at this speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And especially, please avoid overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You need to pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Guilty as charged, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, you mentioned the -- that you didn't know that General Tolimir had been at Srebrenica at the time. And let me put this question to you: Would General Tolimir - and this is going directly to your statement here - would he have had to have been on the ground in Srebrenica, as General Mladic was, in order for you to have made this statement? In other words, would your assessment, as expressed here, change if you were to learn that General Tolimir was not on the ground at certain periods of time? And let's just say in Srebrenica, for example.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't. I'm -- are -- it stopped buzzing. No, it wouldn't. Because the whole business of putting these forward headquarters on the ground is because you, the principal commander, are either in your main headquarters or somewhere else. If Mladic is in Srebrenica, then he doesn't need a -- he is at his own forward headquarters. He doesn't need to put another one forward or another person in it. So -- and all these distances are a day's drive. It's not great distances involved. So it wouldn't surprise me to find that days two and three, for example, Mladic is there, and then a bit later on, he's put someone else, one of his assistant commanders forward into a -- into the area, and he's gone somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so, again, with respect to your statement here that you would expect to find that Tolimir had a significant role in all BSA actions, including Srebrenica, is it your assessment, based on your observations of how the VRS operated and Mladic and Tolimir, watching them personally how they operated, that Tolimir's role would have been any less significant, as you've described it, with respect to Srebrenica, were he not on the ground at a particular place or particular time when some of these critical events are happening?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can measure significance of a particular action, but his particular portfolio would have made -- you know, was what -- dealing with the aftermath of the -- the actual taking of the pocket. And the security issues and so forth would have fallen, directly, as I understand it, into his portfolio.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I thank the Trial Chamber for the additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, are you tendering the last document?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No I'm not, Mr. President. That's the 26-page witness statement of General Smith. If my friends wish to introduce it later, I'll have no objection. But at this point I'm not sure we need to burden e-court. I read out the relevant sections, so I'm not tendering it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, you have nearly five minutes left, but I think it is more convenient to commence the cross-examination tomorrow. But Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just need some clarification to understand some of the goings-on, since you were the high command of the UN in the relevant area. The first question I have is: Who was -- or which parties were involved in the evacuation of the civilian population in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which parties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes. Like your office, the Muslim army or the Serbian armies. That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll take it, as it were, a -- group by group. In -- you have two groups of people involved with me as UNPROFOR. There are the civil affairs staff, who, as I've explained, are reporting to Pedauye and so on, and myself. In addition, and -- a completely independent body of the ICRC are there on the ground, and we have some press, I think, acting on a pool basis of everybody, from the CNN there. I don't recall whether the UNHCR had a detachment in the pocket, but they were certainly involved at the Sarajevo end of the -- of the business. That, if you like, was the UN component, both civil and military. Then you have the Bosnian Serb elements, who were either or represented by Mladic or General Tolimir, depending on the time of these events, and then you have the Bosnians themselves. They are -- you can understand them in two groups. The military component of them led by a man whose name began with P and it's now forgotten, but perhaps someone can help me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, nobody can help you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name began with P. And I am a -- Palic, perhaps, but it's just slipped my mind. I may be able to remember it tomorrow morning. And the civil element whose initial representative was the doctor, Torlak, who I met in Sarajevo when he brought out a busload of wounded people. And others were -- became involved speaking for that group of people. Those were all the, if you like, the people in the mix.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. I have a few questions, but maybe in view of the time, I can continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's your ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have to adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow in the morning at 9.00 in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of March, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m.,
